title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
summary: Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
statement:
Return the maximum depth of the binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.

Trees in the tests are written in level order with `null` for a missing child, so `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` has root 3, children 9 and 20, and 20 has children 15 and 7.
hints: The depth of a tree is 1 + the larger depth of its two subtrees.
Write it recursively: maxDepth(null) = 0, otherwise 1 + max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right)).
An iterative alternative counts levels with a breadth-first search.
explain: The longest root-to-leaf path is 3 → 20 → 15 (or 3 → 20 → 7), which has 3 nodes. So the depth is 3.

title: Same Tree
summary: Return whether two binary trees have the same shape and the same values.
statement:
Return `true` if the binary trees `p` and `q` are the same: they have exactly the same shape and every pair of corresponding nodes has the same value.

For example `[1,2]` and `[1,null,2]` hold the same values but are different shapes (2 is a left child in one and a right child in the other), so they are not the same.
hints: Two trees are the same if their roots match and their left subtrees are the same and their right subtrees are the same.
Handle the base cases first: both null is true; exactly one null is false.
Then compare the values and recurse on (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right).
explain: Both trees have root 1 with left child 2 and right child 3, so they match node for node and the answer is `true`.

title: Invert Binary Tree
summary: Mirror the tree (swap every node's left and right children) and return its root.
statement:
Invert the binary tree, which means mirroring it: swap the left and right child of every node. Return the root.

Trees are given and returned in level order, with `null` for a missing child. Recursively invert both subtrees and then swap them.
hints: Mirroring a tree means mirroring both subtrees and then swapping them.
Recursively invert the left and right subtrees, then swap the two pointers.
Any traversal works as long as every node gets its children swapped exactly once; a queue-based BFS is the iterative version.
explain: Swapping the children of every node makes 7 the left child of 4 and 2 the right child; under them 9, 6 and 3, 1 swap too. Read in level order that is `[4,7,2,9,6,3,1]`.

title: Symmetric Tree
summary: Return whether the tree is a mirror image of itself around its centre.
statement:
Return `true` if the binary tree is symmetric around its centre, meaning the left subtree is a mirror image of the right subtree.

Compare the two subtrees in mirror fashion: the left child of one with the right child of the other, and vice versa.
hints: Compare two subtrees at a time: are they mirror images of each other?
Two trees a and b mirror each other if a.val == b.val, a.left mirrors b.right, and a.right mirrors b.left.
Start with isMirror(root.left, root.right). Both null is true; exactly one null is false.
explain: The root's two children are both 2. Their children read 3, 4 on the left and 4, 3 on the right, which is the mirror image, so the answer is `true`.

title: Path Sum
summary: Return whether some root-to-leaf path has values summing to targetSum.
statement:
Return `true` if the tree has a root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to `targetSum`. A leaf is a node with no children.

An empty tree has no paths, so the answer for it is `false`.

The path must end at a leaf: stopping partway down at a node that still has children does not count, even if the running sum matches.
hints: As you walk down, subtract each node's value from the target that remains.
At a leaf, check whether the remaining target equals the leaf's value.
Only stop at real leaves (both children null). A node with one child is not the end of a path, which is why [1,2] with target 1 is false.
explain: The path 5 → 4 → 11 → 2 ends at a leaf and adds up to 5 + 4 + 11 + 2 = 22, so the answer is `true`.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
summary: Return whether, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one.
statement:
A binary tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Return `true` if the tree is height-balanced.

Compute heights bottom-up and stop as soon as some node is unbalanced; recomputing heights from every node separately costs O(n²).
hints: Checking the heights from the top, at every node, recomputes heights again and again (O(n²) on a skewed tree).
Compute heights bottom-up instead: a function that returns the height of a subtree, or −1 if it is unbalanced.
If either child returns −1, or their heights differ by more than 1, return −1; otherwise return 1 + max. The tree is balanced if the root does not return −1.
explain: At the root the left subtree (just 9) has height 1 and the right subtree (20 with two children) has height 2, a difference of 1. Every other node is also within 1, so the answer is `true`.

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
summary: A node is good if no node on the path from the root to it has a greater value. Count the good nodes.
statement:
A node `X` is good if no node on the path from the root to `X` has a value greater than `X`'s value. The root is always good.

Return the number of good nodes in the tree.

Walk down the tree carrying the largest value seen so far on the path: a node is good when its value is at least that maximum.
hints: Whether a node is good depends only on the largest value seen on the path above it.
Do a DFS that passes down the maximum so far.
A node is good when node.val ≥ maxSoFar; pass max(maxSoFar, node.val) to the children and add up the counts.
explain: The good nodes are the root 3, the 4, the 3 under the 1 (the path 3, 1, 3 has nothing bigger than 3), and the 5. The two 1s each have a 3 above them. That is 4 good nodes.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
summary: Return the lowest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). The tests give p and q by value (values are unique); the judge prints the value of the node you return.
call: TreeNode t = BCBT.T($0); Object r = BCBT.val(s.lowestCommonAncestor(t, BCBT.find(t, BCB.I($1)), BCBT.find(t, BCB.I($2))));
statement:
Return the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of the nodes with values `p` and `q`: the lowest node in the tree that has both of them as descendants, where a node counts as a descendant of itself.

All values are unique, `p != q`, and both are in the tree. The tests give `p` and `q` as values; the judge prints the value of the node you return.
constraints: All values are unique; p and q are in the tree and differ
hints: Ask each subtree: "do you contain p or q?" and pass the answer up.
Recurse: if the current node is p or q, return it. Otherwise look in both subtrees.
If both sides return a node, the current node is the LCA. If only one side does, return that side's result.
explain: Node 5 is in the root's left subtree and node 1 is in its right subtree, so the deepest node that has both below it is the root, 3.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
summary: Rebuild the binary tree (unique values) from its preorder and inorder traversals and return its root.
statement:
`preorder` and `inorder` are the preorder and inorder traversals of the same binary tree, whose values are all distinct. Build the tree and return its root.

The answer is returned in level order with `null` for a missing child. A hash map from value to inorder index avoids searching for the root each time.
hints: The first value of preorder is the root. Where does that value sit in inorder?
Everything left of the root in inorder is the left subtree; everything right of it is the right subtree. Their sizes tell you how to split preorder too.
Use a HashMap from value to inorder index and recurse on index ranges, consuming preorder from left to right. That is O(n) instead of O(n²).
explain: Preorder starts with the root, 3. In inorder, 9 is left of 3 and 15, 20, 7 are right of it, so 9 is the left subtree and 20 (next in preorder) roots the right one with children 15 and 7. In level order that is `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
summary: Design Codec: serialize(root) turns a tree into a string, deserialize(data) rebuilds the same tree. Any format works. The judge serialises with one Codec, deserialises with another, and prints the rebuilt tree.
call: Codec ser = new Codec(), deser = new Codec(); Object r = deser.deserialize(ser.serialize(BCBT.T($0))); if (r == null) r = new ArrayList<>();

perf.label: a tree of 100,000 nodes
perf.call: TreeNode t = BCBT.random(BCB.perm(100000, 0)); Codec ser = new Codec(), de = new Codec(); Object r = de.deserialize(ser.serialize(t));

statement:
Design a `Codec` with two methods:

- `String serialize(TreeNode root)` turns a binary tree into a string,
- `TreeNode deserialize(String data)` turns that string back into the same tree.

You choose the format. The judge serialises with one `Codec` object, deserialises with a second one, and prints the rebuilt tree, so the string must carry everything.
hints: A preorder traversal alone is ambiguous, but it becomes unambiguous if you also write a marker for every null child.
serialize: preorder DFS writing "val," for a node and "#," for null. deserialize: read tokens in order, recursively building root, left, then right.
Use a StringBuilder, not string concatenation, and avoid deep recursion for very tall trees (or build iteratively), since a 10⁵-node chain is possible.
explain: The tests turn the tree into a string with your serialize, rebuild it with your deserialize, and compare. The rebuilt tree must be the same as the original, `[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]`.

title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
summary: Return the values of the tree in inorder: left subtree, then the node, then right subtree.
statement:
Return the **inorder** traversal of the tree's values: for every node, first everything in its left subtree, then the node itself, then everything in its right subtree.

Follow-up: the recursive solution is short. Can you do it iteratively?
hints: Recursively: traverse(left), add the node, traverse(right).
Iteratively, a stack replaces the call stack. Go as far left as you can, pushing each node you pass.
Pop a node, record it, then move to its right child and repeat the "go left" step. Stop when both the current pointer is null and the stack is empty.
explain: Node 1 has no left child, so it comes first. Then its right subtree: 2 has left child 3, so 3 comes before 2. The answer is `[1,3,2]`.

title: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
summary: Return the values of the tree in preorder: the node, then left subtree, then right subtree.
statement:
Return the **preorder** traversal of the tree's values: for every node, first the node itself, then everything in its left subtree, then everything in its right subtree.

Follow-up: can you do it iteratively?
hints: Recursively: add the node, traverse(left), traverse(right).
Iteratively, pop a node from a stack, record it and push its children.
Push the right child before the left one, so the left child is popped (and visited) first.
explain: Preorder visits 1 first, then its right subtree rooted at 2, where 2 comes before its left child 3. The answer is `[1,2,3]`.

title: Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
summary: Return the values of the tree in postorder: left subtree, then right subtree, then the node.
statement:
Return the **postorder** traversal of the tree's values: for every node, first everything in its left subtree, then everything in its right subtree, then the node itself.

Follow-up: can you do it iteratively?
hints: Recursively: traverse(left), traverse(right), add the node.
Postorder reversed is "node, right, left", which is just preorder with the children swapped.
Run that modified preorder with a stack (push left, then right) and reverse the result, or add each value to the front of the list.
explain: Postorder finishes the deepest node first: 3 (left child of 2), then 2, then the root 1. The answer is `[3,2,1]`.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
summary: Return true if root contains a subtree identical to subRoot: some node of root together with all of its descendants, same structure and values.
statement:
Return `true` if `root` contains a subtree with exactly the same structure and node values as `subRoot`, and `false` otherwise.

A subtree of `root` is a node of `root` together with **all** of its descendants. `root` counts as a subtree of itself.

For example, if node 2 had an extra child 0 underneath, the subtree at 4 would no longer match, because a subtree must include every descendant.
hints: Write a helper sameTree(a, b) that checks whether two trees are identical.
Then try every node of root as a starting point: isSubtree(root) = sameTree(root, subRoot) || isSubtree(root.left) || isSubtree(root.right).
That is O(m · n). For O(m + n), serialise both trees with markers for null children and between values (like ",4,1,#,#,2,#,#"), then search for one string in the other with KMP.
explain: The node 4 in `root` has children 1 and 2 and nothing below them, which is exactly `subRoot`, so the answer is `true`.

title: Construct Quad Tree
summary: Build the quad tree of an n × n grid of 0s and 1s: a region whose cells are all equal is a leaf with that value; otherwise it splits into four quarters. The output lists [isLeaf, val] per node in level order.
statement:
`grid` is an `n × n` matrix of 0s and 1s, where `n` is a power of 2. Represent it as a **quad tree** and return the root.

Each quad tree node has `val` (true for 1, false for 0) and `isLeaf`, plus four children `topLeft`, `topRight`, `bottomLeft` and `bottomRight`. To build the node for a square region:

- if every cell in the region has the same value, the node is a leaf: `isLeaf = true`, `val` = that value, and no children;
- otherwise `isLeaf = false` (`val` can be anything) and the region is split into four equal quarters, each built the same way.

The output lists the nodes level by level as `[isLeaf, val]` (1 for true, 0 for false), writing `null` for the missing children of leaves, as LeetCode does. Inner nodes are shown with `val = 1`, whatever you set.
constraints: n is a power of 2 between 1 and 64
hints: Write build(row, col, size) for the square starting at (row, col). A 1 × 1 square is always a leaf.
Top-down: if all cells in the square are equal, return a leaf; otherwise recurse on the four quarters. Checking every square costs O(n²) per level, O(n² log n) in total.
Bottom-up is O(n²): build the four quarters first, and if all four are leaves with the same value, merge them into one leaf instead of creating an inner node.
explain: The 2 × 2 grid mixes 0s and 1s, so the root is an inner node, shown as [0,1]. Each quarter is a single cell and so a leaf: 0, 1, 1, 0. The output is `[[0,1],[1,0],[1,1],[1,1],[1,0]]`.

title: Delete Leaves With a Given Value
summary: Delete every leaf whose value is target. Keep going: a parent that becomes a leaf with value target is deleted too. Return the remaining tree.
statement: Delete every **leaf** node whose value is `target`. If deleting a leaf turns its parent into a leaf with value `target`, delete the parent too, and keep going until no such leaf is left. Return the root of the remaining tree (which may be empty).
hints: Whether a node becomes a leaf depends on what happens to its children first. Which traversal order handles children before their parent?
Postorder: recursively clean the left and right subtrees and assign the results back to root.left and root.right.
After that, if root has no children and root.val == target, return null; otherwise return root. One pass handles the chain reaction.
explain: The leaves with value 2 (under node 2 on the left, and under node 3) are deleted. The left 2 then becomes a leaf with value 2, so it goes too. What is left is 1 → 3 → 4: `[1,null,3,null,4]`.
